name: Justo L. González
place: Cuba, Puerto Rico, and the United States
title: Justo L. González: telling the story of the church in our own language
description: A Cuban historian and his work to bring Christian history and theological education closer to Spanish-speaking readers.

sections.heading: Learning to explain clearly
paragraphs: Justo Luis González was born in Havana in 1937. His mother was an educator and the author of grammar books; his father worked writing materials that readers without specialized training could understand. The biography from his resource center connects that family setting with his interest in explaining complex matters in an accessible way.

He studied at the Evangelical Theological Seminary in Matanzas and was ordained a Methodist minister in 1957. He then earned a doctorate in historical theology at Yale. His training linked institutions in Cuba and the United States, before a period of teaching church history in Puerto Rico.

sections.heading: Forming readers and opening opportunities
paragraphs: He taught for eight years at the Evangelical Seminary of Puerto Rico and later at Candler, at Emory University. His works include Historia del cristianismo and Historia del pensamiento cristiano. These books are part of a career that has brought debates, people, and events closer to readers in different languages.

His service also includes developing initiatives in Hispanic theological education, among them the Hispanic Summer Program, the Association for Hispanic Theological Education, and the Hispanic Theological Initiative. The work of a historian thus appears alongside the forming of communities that need to study and teach from their own context.

reflection: Second Timothy 2:2 speaks of entrusting what we have learned to people who are able to teach others. Christian teaching has a generational dimension: we receive, examine, and share. A clear explanation can open a door for someone who used to think that studying history or theology was beyond their reach.

Reading church history calls for gratitude and discernment. Knowing an interpretation does not oblige us to accept all of it; it does ask us to understand what it says and to compare it with the sources. Preparing a lesson, explaining a term, and listening to the group’s questions are everyday ways of serving with what we have learned.
review_note: A profile based on the biography from his resource center. His training and service are described without presenting all of his theological interpretations as Verbo’s position. No statements are added about his current personal situation.
source_labels: Justo & Catherine González Resource Center. “Dr. Justo L. González.”
